title: Psoriatic arthritis in later life and frailty (UK)

direct_answer: Psoriatic arthritis can start or continue into later life, causing painful, swollen joints, tendon pain and fatigue alongside psoriasis. In older or frail people, treatment choices take account of other conditions, infection risk and medicines. Regular review, exercise and good skin and foot care help.

content:
Psoriatic arthritis is a type of inflammatory arthritis that affects some people with psoriasis. It usually starts between the ages of 30 and 50, but it can continue for many years and can sometimes begin later in life. In older age, it can overlap with frailty, osteoarthritis and other conditions.

This guide explains how psoriatic arthritis can affect older people, what to think about with treatment, and practical ways to stay well. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

Symptoms

The NHS lists symptoms including joint pain, stiffness and swelling. Other features can include swelling of a whole finger or toe (dactylitis), pain where tendons attach to bone, such as the heel, nail changes and tiredness. Symptoms often come and go in flares.

How it overlaps with frailty

Pain, fatigue and inflammation can reduce activity, which can lead to weaker muscles and slower walking. Foot and heel pain can affect balance. It can be hard to tell whether a change is a flare, osteoarthritis or general frailty, so tell your team about new or different symptoms.

Treatment in later life

Treatment aims to control inflammation and protect joints. It may include anti-inflammatory medicines, steroid injections, disease-modifying medicines such as methotrexate, and biological or targeted medicines. In older people, your team will consider your kidney function, other medicines, infection risk and vaccinations. Regular blood tests may be needed. Never stop or change medicines without advice.

Staying active

  • Gentle, regular exercise helps stiffness, strength and mood.
  • Seated or water-based exercise may be easier on painful feet and joints.
  • Pace activities across the day, especially during flares.

Skin, nails and feet

  • Keep skin moisturised and follow your psoriasis treatment plan.
  • Ask for podiatry if nail changes or foot pain make walking hard.
  • Choose supportive, well-fitting shoes.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can psoriatic arthritis start in older age?

It usually starts earlier, but it can begin later. New joint swelling in later life should be assessed.

Are biologics safe for older people?

They can be used, but your team will weigh the benefits against risks such as infection.

Will vaccines help?

Vaccines such as flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal and shingles may be recommended. Ask your team which are suitable with your treatment.
